content.title: WHY YOUR {{MEAL PREP}} IS QUIETLY WASTING ALL THAT NUTRITION
facts: **Storing rice warm** – Putting hot rice straight into a sealed container traps steam, creating a moist environment where bacteria can multiply fast; let it cool for about 30 minutes uncovered first.
**Microwaving in plastic** – Reheating meal-prep containers in the microwave can cause compounds from the plastic to leach into your food, especially with fatty sauces; switch to glass or ceramic.
**Draining canned beans and tossing the liquid** – You're pouring out fiber-rich starch and some B vitamins along with the aquafaba; a quick rinse keeps more nutrients than a full dump-and-drain.
**Adding lemon juice too early** – Squeezing citrus into a salad long before eating wilts greens and breaks down vitamin C over time; dress it right before serving instead.
**Pressure-cooking everything the same way** – Overcooking vegetables in a pressure cooker past the recommended time breaks down water-soluble vitamins like B and C far more than steaming briefly.

**Freezing meals in thick glass containers** – Rapid temperature changes can crack glass and also slow even freezing, letting ice crystals form that damage texture and some nutrients; use shallow, freezer-safe containers.
**Reusing the same oil for frying** – Oil that's been heated multiple times breaks down and forms compounds that aren't great for your body; stick to one or two uses max for frying oils.
**Prepping leafy greens days in advance** – Pre-chopped spinach or kale loses folate and vitamin C quickly once cut; chop closer to cooking day when possible.

content.caption:
A few of these meal-prep habits are so normal they don't even feel like mistakes. Take rice: when you seal it up while it's still steaming hot, the trapped moisture becomes a perfect breeding ground for Bacillus cereus, a bacteria that survives reheating and can cause stomach issues hours later. Then there's lemon juice — vitamin C is sensitive to air and light, so once you squeeze it onto cut vegetables or greens, oxidation starts breaking it down within the hour, not days. And canned beans: most of us drain and rinse out of habit, but that liquid carries resistant starch that feeds good gut bacteria, so rinsing too aggressively washes away more benefit than people realize. Everyone's kitchen setup is different, so adjust what fits your routine.
